blocks.text: 1. Types of Machine Learning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442847371-697051057.png

What Is Machine Learning, the previous topic, introduced the core recipe underlying every Machine Learning system: data, a model, a training process, and a trained model capable of making predictions. That recipe actually branches into several genuinely distinct types, depending on what kind of data is available and what the actual goal is.

Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-Supervised, and Reinforcement Learning are the four major types, each covered in its own dedicated topic immediately following this one. Choosing the right type for a given problem is genuinely the very first decision that needs to be made in any real Machine Learning project, well before any specific algorithm gets chosen.
2. Supervised Learning, Previewed
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442847372-938497699.png

Supervised Learning means learning from labeled examples, where every single training example already comes with the correct answer attached directly to it. Predicting a house's price from a set of examples where the true, actual price is already known for each one is a classic, clear illustration of this type.

This is the type covered in the very next topic, and it is generally the most common starting point for a first Machine Learning project, since having clear, correct answers already available makes both training and evaluating a model considerably more straightforward.
3. Unsupervised Learning, Previewed
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442847372-784693187.png

Unsupervised Learning means learning from unlabeled examples, where no correct answer is provided at all, and the system instead has to find genuine structure entirely on its own. Grouping customers into natural segments, with no predefined categories handed to the system in advance, is a classic illustration of this type.

This type genuinely suits situations where the goal is discovering unknown structure or patterns, rather than predicting one specific, already-known answer, a distinction covered in far more depth in its own dedicated topic.
4. Semi-Supervised Learning, Previewed
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442847635-265747009.png

Semi-Supervised Learning occupies a genuinely practical middle ground between the two previous types, combining a small number of labeled examples with a much larger pool of unlabeled ones. This fits situations where labeling is genuinely expensive or slow, so only a modest subset of examples ever actually gets labeled by hand.

This approach lets a system benefit from the structure present in a large amount of unlabeled data, while still anchoring its learning to the smaller, more reliable set of labeled examples that are actually available, a genuinely practical compromise covered in full in its own topic.
5. Reinforcement Learning, Previewed
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442847637-707911518.png

Reinforcement Learning means learning through trial, error, and reward, with no labeled examples involved at all. Instead, an agent takes actions within some environment and receives feedback on how good, or bad, those actions actually turned out to be.

A game-playing agent that improves purely through repeated play, guided by reward signals rather than any labeled correct move, is a classic illustration of this type, a genuinely different learning setup from the other three, covered in full in its own dedicated topic.

blocks.text: 6. The Single Deciding Question
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442847637-535858568.png

A single, genuinely useful question determines which type actually fits a given problem: do labeled, correct answers already exist for the data at hand? If yes, for every single example, Supervised Learning is the natural fit. If yes, but only for some examples, Semi-Supervised Learning fits considerably better.

If no labels exist at all, and the actual goal is simply finding structure, Unsupervised Learning is the right choice. If no labels exist, but the problem instead involves taking actions and receiving feedback over time, Reinforcement Learning is the right fit. Asking this one question first considerably narrows down which of the four types is actually worth exploring further for any given problem.
7. Real Systems Often Blend Types

This connects back to the everyday examples already covered in the What Is Machine Learning topic. A streaming recommendation system, for instance, often blends Supervised and Unsupervised techniques together in practice, rather than relying on just one single type in complete isolation.

A real, deployed product rarely maps cleanly onto just one of these four categories, understanding each type individually, exactly the purpose of this topic and the four that follow it, is what makes it possible to recognize how a real system actually combines them together to solve its own particular problem.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Recognizing which type, or blend of types, a real system actually uses is a genuinely useful skill on its own, worth practicing as this course introduces more concrete algorithms in the modules ahead.

blocks.text: 8. What Actually Drives the Choice in Practice

blocks.alt: What Actually Drives the Choice in Practice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442847638-862855778.png

In practice, what actually drives which type gets chosen often comes down to data availability and the nature of the problem itself. Labeled data that is expensive or slow to collect favors Unsupervised or Semi-Supervised approaches, since these types make better use of data that has not already been manually labeled.

A problem with no single correct answer, only a sequence of decisions to make over time, favors Reinforcement Learning instead. And clear labeled examples already existing in abundance favors Supervised Learning, generally the most direct, reliable starting point whenever that kind of data is genuinely available.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Choosing a Machine Learning type based on what sounds most impressive, rather than what the actual available data and problem genuinely call for, is a common mistake worth avoiding from the very start of any real project.

blocks.text: 9. Where This Course Goes Next

This topic has previewed all four major types at a high level. Supervised Learning, covered in its own topic immediately next, is the natural starting point given how common labeled data actually is in most real projects. Unsupervised Learning follows directly after that.

Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning are then covered in turn, each in genuine depth, with its own concrete examples and its own particular tradeoffs. By the end of these four topics, every major branch of Machine Learning introduced here will have been covered thoroughly enough to recognize, and reason about, in a real, practical project.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below illustrates the core distinction between Supervised and Unsupervised Learning directly, using the exact same small dataset for both.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X = np.array([[25, 40000], [45, 80000], [30, 45000], [50, 90000], [22, 38000], [48, 85000]])

labels = np.array([0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1])  # 0 = did not buy, 1 = bought, known for every example
supervised_model = LogisticRegression()
supervised_model.fit(X, labels)
print("Supervised Learning: trained using known, correct labels for every example")
print(f"Predicted class for a new customer: {supervised_model.predict([[35, 60000]])}")

unsupervised_model = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=42, n_init=10)
cluster_assignments = unsupervised_model.fit_predict(X)
print("\nUnsupervised Learning: no labels given at all, the system found its own grouping")
print(f"Discovered cluster assignments: {cluster_assignments}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Notice the Supervised model was given the correct answer for every training example, while the Unsupervised model received no answers at all and instead discovered its own grouping directly from the data's structure.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Machine Learning branches into Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-Supervised, and Reinforcement Learning.
Supervised Learning trains on labeled examples where the correct answer is already known for every case.
Unsupervised Learning finds structure with no correct answer provided at all.
Semi-Supervised Learning combines a small labeled set with a much larger unlabeled pool.
Reinforcement Learning has an agent learn through trial, error, and reward feedback, not labeled examples.
Whether labels exist, and for how many examples, is the single deciding question for which type fits a problem.
Real systems, like recommendation engines, often blend multiple types together rather than relying on just one.
Data availability and the problem's own shape, not what sounds impressive, should drive which type actually gets chosen.
Next up: Supervised Learning, covered in full depth as the first of the four major types.
